text: Undergraduate students are generally price-sensitive and are more likely to consider a product when it offers a free tier, student pricing, or a clearly demonstrated value for money.
Students are more willing to spend time or money on tools that they believe can improve their technical skills, strengthen their portfolio, or increase their chances of getting an internship.
Students often have limited time because of lectures, assignments, examinations, projects, and extracurricular activities. Tools that reduce effort or save time are therefore attractive.
Students tend to prefer tools that are easy to understand and require little setup. A technically powerful product may be rejected if it has a complicated onboarding process.
Students are more likely to trust a new technology product when they can see demonstrations, examples, reviews, or evidence that it works in realistic situations.

Technology-oriented students are generally familiar with AI tools and may be interested in experimenting with new AI products, but they may compare a new tool with existing free alternatives before adopting it.
Students often prefer practical learning experiences such as projects, interactive examples, coding exercises, and real-world applications over purely theoretical explanations.
When evaluating a new student-focused product, students may consider usefulness, cost, time required, ease of use, career relevance, and whether similar functionality is already available elsewhere.
